November 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 3
We had another great turnout last month! I counted 75 people in the Hall. Was it the prize draw?
Was it a chance to show off your favourite work?
Or maybe our feature presenter, Marco Berera
drew our members through the door. Marco is always insightful and entertaining with his interesting
approach to making things. It was great to welcome
back some people that we have not seen for a
while. I also note several new faces! Welcome to
our club.
Thank you to Art Liestman for telling our story during part II of our 25th Anniversary. Art packed a lot
of our history into a short time and hopefully this
will inspire our newer members to get involved and
make things happen. Thank you to Peter Hill, Bill
Fowle, and Dustin Cook for organizing the last two
meetings. It takes a village to run our organization!
Grumblings… We all know that parking is crummy
around Sapperton Hall. Please be a part of the solution by not blocking off open spots in the Hall parking lot. If you need a quick getaway, you can find
street parking on Keary Street and Simpson Street.
Thank you kindly!
January’s president’s challenge is “musical” - something that is part of an instrument. You can think
percussion, strings - anything that you might find in
a band or orchestra.
Steve

Last month’s call for more article certainly bore
fruit this month! I’m over the moon with the many
excellent article submissions this month. Let’s
keep them coming as we go into the New Year!
I’m so happy to announce that Bruce Campbell is
back with his monthly Tech Talk roundup!
Allan Cusworth has provided a detailed account of
Marco’s October demonstration of turning fish,
including the handouts that Marco mentioned during his presentation. Allan has also provided an excellent article on making drawbars for our lathes.
Cathy Friesen has shared her experience making a
Baby room nightlight with a Turkish glass globe.
Pippa Lattey shares the results of our Summer
Swap Collaboration Exchange that took place during our summer break.
David Sweet has secured permission for us to reprint
Todd Hoyer's comprehensive handout on predicting and maximizing grain patterns when cutting
turning blanks.
We also have a detailed account by The Westside
Wood Whackers about their collaboration on a
large Maple Burl footed bowl.
Don Gamble reviews his Stuart Batty grinding
platform and Dustin Cook talks about his recent
visit to the Honolulu Woodturner's Club.
Our Member Profile this month features Brian Andrews.
We also have a larger than usual Instant Gallery
from last month's 25th Anniversary Gallery.
Steve

November 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 4
Diana asked for advice on how to rearrange her
shop to make her lathe more accessible. Larry suggested that placing it at a 45° angle to the wall accommodates easier access to the rear for cleaning
and also for those who were strongly left-handed.
Fraser shared an interesting solution to a longstanding problem. Apparently the threads on the
end of a Dremel tool, which allows you to attach
various accessories, is a nonstandard thread and he
wanted to build a block that he could use as a holder while doing off-lathe decorations. After Frasier
had acquired a 3D printer, he started looking into
software that would help him with that problem.
He showed us an interesting block that he modeled
with a threaded hole in which he could thread the
nose of a Dremel. The CAD software that he used is
called Tinker CAD and it exports an STL file for his
3D printer. He showed us an online example. It is
quite intuitive rather than scanning things. This exploding market of 3D printers and powerful modeling tools is adding an entire new dimension in what
we can do in our turning world.
Larry asked about alcohol drying. That is taking a
green piece of wood, freshly turned, and soaking it
in high concentration of alcohol and then allowing
it to dry. The theory being that the alcohol displaces the water and allows the alcohol to flash off
when you remove it from the liquid. I’ve tried this
method myself, but I find there are several significant limitations to it. First, it’s hard to scale. That is,
to do a large number of pieces at the same time.
Alcohol dilutes as it absorbs the water from the
wood thus making it less effective for the next
batch and the material itself is quite dangerous. It
is highly flammable and, when absorbed through
the skin, does nasty things to your body. In addition, highly purified anhydrous alcohol is hard to
get your hands on. What you can get is often
mixed with boron to aid in the displacing of the final bits of water and that makes it even more poisonous. My advice is don’t mess with alcohol as a
drying method. You can look at a number of different articles in our newsletter archive on various
treatment methods. The best of which is to boil
the wood before you allow it to dry. It speeds the
drying process and reduces warping.
The next question we dealt with was how to finish
a piece of not yet dry wood that has been turned
green. Consensus was generally agreed that using
oil is a better option than something that might
seal the fibers such as wipe on poly. A drying oil
could be used such as tung oil, but a simpler solution is to simply use mineral oil.
Fraser showed us a unique way to manage small
quantities of epoxy glue. Instead of mixing them
on a flat surface like a piece of card stock, he recommends filling a small Ziploc bag with equal
amounts by weight, closing the Ziploc bag and
kneading the materials together as required. Then

Small plastic bags are readily available at dollar

Brian showed a unique way to repair a sink in his
house using old cross-country ski.
Our kitchen faucet was hard to grab hold of, so I
turned a grab ring.
My first choice was to use maple and saturated it
with Varathane Wood Hardner in a vacuum chamber. Once again, Mother Nature won that battle.
Water still managed to get in and split the growth
rings apart after several months of use.
For the new version, I used
an old pair of cross-country
skis that had delaminated
and
turned
something
round.
After the turning was done I put it on a jamb chuck
to give it a coating of epoxy.
Just before the epoxy fully
cured, I put my fingerprints all over it to make
the glossy finish turn into
a matte finish.
Now I have a new kitchen
sink faucet part that will
never rust, split open on a
growth ring and know
every time I use it, I will be
reminded of my old repurposed skis. Who knows
where else this old ski material will show up after
being on my lathe.

Marco Berera is a world class woodturner who has
been a member of the Greater Vancouver
Woodturners Guild since its inception in September 1999. Over the years he has spent untold hours
helping other turners perfect their turning skills
using safe and efficient methods.
At our meeting on October 24, Marco used his
knowledge, skills and dry humour to show us all
how to turn fish on a woodturning lathe. The turning method he used is categorized as Therming.
Therming is an ancient style of woodturning that
Marco learned from Sigi Angerer, a Swiss professional woodturner he met in Olberhau, Germany at
a woodturning symposium. They met again when
Sigi came to Seattle for a demonstration, and yet
again when he came to Provo, Utah woodturning
symposium where Marco translated Sigi’s demonstrations. These occasions were a special time for
him, I’m sure.
Therming is a method of turning a number of identical pieces on a special lathe fixture that allows
many turning blanks to be mounted together.
Marco used that principle to turn his fish.
Marco started his demonstration with a discussion
and slides about his turning history which began as
an apprentice in Switzerland. He followed that by
describing the blanks and mounting fixtures that he
uses to turn two identical fish.
The blanks are two pieces of 1” x 2” wood that,
(Continued on page 7)
Marco at the lathe
Fixtures and Blanks

November 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 7
when mounted together, become 2” x 2” turning
blank. The blank lengths are different depending
on the size and type of fish to be made. The blanks
are not glued together.
Marco has made a special tailstock fixture that
threads onto the live centre. Pieces of plywood are
glued together and attached to a hub that is
threaded onto the live centre. The front of the fixture is a recess made to fit the 2” square blank
snugly and tapered slightly to force the two 1” x 2”
components together and crush the corners a little
bit thereby ensuring a tight fit. The 2” blank is
clamped tightly in the jaws of a scroll chuck in the
headstock. The assembly is now ready for turning.
Using a skew chisel, Marco formed the shape of
one side of the two fish. He then rotated the two
1” x 2” blanks, clamped them back between the
tailstock fixture and the scroll chuck and proceeded
to shape the opposite side. He made sure that we
understood that when cutting using the therming
process, you will be cutting a lot of air. A faster
lathe speed may produce a smoother cut. Marco’s
handouts (at end of article) describe the steps Sigi
and Marco use to form the fish. It would be repetition to duplicate those steps here.
Marco showed us that there are almost unlimited
variations of fish that can be made with this turning method and jigs.
Marco’s showed is that his turned fish can be happy, or sad; small or large. The choice is up to you.
He even showed us one fish that had a hammer
through its eye socket. He called that one a Hammer-fsh since it had no eye! (I told you he has a dry
sense of humour!
Thank you, Marco for a very interesting and different style of turning wood. Hopefully our members

This summer our son and daughter-in-law surprised us with the wonderful news that they were
expecting a baby. Of course the wheels in my head
started turning as to what I would make for the
baby’s room.
I had recently attended a workshop on how to
make a Turkish lamp at a beautiful shop in New
Westminster.
https://vancouver.mosaicartstudio.ca/
I chose to make just a glass globe with the idea of
turning my own base.
I found a pretty piece of cherry from the wood that
I won in Barry Wilkinson’s raffle and made the
base.
The light is a small LED bulb which doesn’t generate any heat but I still made a pierced top to let the
light shine through and any heat, if any, escape.
When the light is turned off, the white plaster
(Continued on page 11)

An easy hack to keep your zap straps from spilling
everywhere.
Cut a “V” hole on the side of the bag and leave the
top and bottom sealed.
When you need a strap just pull one out of the side
through the “v” hole.
The rest of the straps stay in the bag.
Do you have a Shop Hack that makes your life easier in your studio/workshop? Share it with others
by emailing it to editor@gvwg.ca

In May, I returned from the AAW Symposium in
Portland Oregon energized by the connections I
made, and bursting with ideas. One activity that I
missed out on was an Instagram collaborative challenge. It was organized by Marie Anderson, who is
also a WIT committee member and involved in the
WIT exchange. For this symposium challenge, participants brought an unfinished piece to the symposium, where they were paired up, and exchanged their piece with their partner. Then they
returned home with a piece to finish. Everyone is
invited to bring their finished pieces to share at the
AAW Symposium next year in Louisville.
I decided to run a smaller local version of this challenge over our summer break, when we do not
have any meetings. Let's call it a Summer Swap,
and let's do it again next summer please!
At our June meeting, twelve intrepid turners
brought in unfinished pieces to contribute. I drew
names in a hat, and paired everyone up. Each
turner took home a piece to work on. The plan was
to share the finished pieces at our first meeting
after the summer break, in September. Our 25th
Anniversary Celebrations took over, so we shared
the results at the October meeting instead. We had
a late entry too, David Sweet and Ed Pretty who
already had the idea for a "Pretty Sweet" collaboration during the symposium.
We're planning to do a Summer Swap again next
summer, open to all GVWG members. Please consider joining in, and start thinking about what kind
of unfinished project you could contribute.
Thank you to all the participants for trusting another turner to finish your piece, and for sharing your
photos and descriptions of your process.
Pippa Lattey + Terry Kennedy
Pippa: I completed Terry's chestnut blank with a
"double rim". I was curious how this would show
off the distinctive grain, a little like a beaded bowl
but with harder edges. I also applied many more
coats of Tung Oil than I usually would, to fill in the
grain and to achieve a nice glossy finish.

Steve brought a hollow form that Don made into a
box with an ebony lid. Here's Don's description:
"The Conversation"
Most people feel this piece is great with just its ebony lid. Some feel strongly that the lid needs a handle. A few like the rock handle, and many others do
not. Once I add a handle or leave it absent, the
piece becomes only a small box.
I've decided that the conversation is a part of the
piece. Therefore, I present a small box with an unaffixed rock handle and ask, "What do you chose?"
Base: maple, finished with Osmo TopOil. Lid: ebony
wax buffed. Unaffixed handle: maple burl, carved,
burned and dry-brushed.
Jim Worden + Chris Stiles
Chris: The piece that I brought in was an unfinished
arbutus wood box that I was using to practice
thread chasing. The box itself was finished and the
threads chased but I had set it aside because I
could not decide on a final shape for the lid. Jim did
quite a nice job of finishing the lid with a shape
that complemented the box.
Jim: I was tasked with making a top on a threaded
box. Chris had made the bottom part of the box
with curved crisp lines. I looked at Chris Stoot’s
book page 52 ( Chinese hat) that could work. The
top part had a big knot in it so I used a 1/4 inch
bowl gouge and a spindle gouge and made light
cuts not too much wood at a time. I back filled the
knot with sawdust and glue, sanded to 400 grit trying to keep the lines crisp. Overall I enjoyed it.

Many of our mature GVWG members will remember an entertaining and highly informative demo
day way back on Saturday, May 3, 2008 at Sapperton Hall when Todd Hoyer and Hayley Smith enlightened us about turning artistic pieces. For example::
https://auction.woodturner.org/Hayley-SmithTodd-Hoyer-Hemisphere-2-1997_i48946691
One of the highlights of the day was a talk by Todd
about how to predict and maximize grain patterns
for various wood species when cutting turning
blanks. The main focus was how to visualize the
best blank with the grain pattern one is looking for
within the parent log. Todd passed out a handout
that illustrated what grain patterns are obtained on
the lathe when a certain blank is cut from a given
log orientation.
This handout has been a valuable resource for me
in my shop since I first received it at the demo day.
I use it often when planning a piece from a blank
I’ve been gifted. And I study it before setting out
for a day of chain sawing.
Recently, I thought other members of the Guild
that didn’t see this demo may also enjoy having a
copy of Todd’s excellent handout. I contacted
Todd at his studio in Arizona and I asked permission from him to reprint it in an edition of our
newsletter. Graciously, Todd agreed and granted
me permission. Please see the next page for the
full handout..
Note: This eight-page handout is copyrighted and
cannot be reproduced in any way without the expressed permission of Todd Hoyer.

The Westside Wood Whackers (WWWs) is a group
of five Guild members who live in Vancouver and
informally get together to harvest wood, support
each other, and work on woodturning projects.
Please see the WWWs’ names above. Our most
recent project was making a maple burl bowl; it
has taken about one year to complete.
The inspiration for the project first started at a
Guild meeting when Gaalen and Olaf came across
a beautiful piece of maple burl that Pat and Denise
Taylor had on display.
Gaalen and Olaf were not sure what the burl was
destined to become, but they knew it was special
and that they had to buy it. They brought it to the
next WWW work session and, after much consideration and discussion, the consensus was to make a
decorative footed-bowl. None of the details were
determined yet, but we knew that we needed to
reshape the burl to start, especially the excess
sticking out from the blank, to create a pleasing,
circular form. We also wanted to retain the natural
beauty of the burl surface, especially the sharp
spikes from under the bark. Rather than turning
the bottom of the bowl we wanted to accentuate
the natural contours of the burl. In order to be
able to appreciate the design, we agreed some sort
of feet would be needed to elevate the bowl for
display.
During this first work session, David trimmed the
excess from the blank to produce a circular shape
and then used large Dremel and Foredom carving
burs to transform the cut edges to match the natural contour of the underside.
After reshaping, he used a combination of yellow
and brown acrylics to darken the lighter, carved

At the next group meeting, we considered whether
we should turn the depression in the centre of the
blank or if it should be offset; whether it should be
a shallow depression or a deep bowl; and whether
the turned edge should be sharp, rounded, or undercut. Once those decisions were made we had
to figure out how to mount an irregularly-shaped
blank with an undulating bottom contour in order
to turn the bowl’s depression in its top flat surface.
We placed a foam pad on a set of Cole jaws in order to stabilize the uneven bottom. To accommodate the thickness of the foam pad plus the uneven
bottom, plus the shape of the burl, we had to modify the Cole jaws. We drilled and threaded four
new 6mm. holes around the edge of the Cole jaws
to attach four threaded bolts with shop-made anchor knobs and hardwood clamping feet. This allowed us to align the blank accurately and hold it
firmly.
We used a framing square to make sure the blank
was at right angles to the bed ways by adjusting
each of the clamping feet as the burl compressed
different areas of the foam pad. The blank was rotated by hand and each blank segment between
the clamps was checked and adjusted as needed.
The knobs were painted red and high-vis tape added to the tool rest to provide better visibility while
the blank was spinning. A depth hole was drilled
and then the bowl was turned using a badger hollower, bowl gouge and scraper. After sanding to
320g, three coats of a shop-made mixture of pol-

The final step in the collaboration was to determine how to “lift” the bowl in order to best display
the character of the burl wood. Some Desert Ironwood from Arizona was available and the colour of
the fine lines within the Ironwood complimented
the burl. It was decided to turn three thin legs
from the Ironwood and have them support the
piece at approximately a 15-degree angle. In order
to insert the legs in the bottom of the bowl, we had
to determine where on the uneven bottom surface
the legs could be placed and holes drilled. The legs
had to be located equidistant from the centre and
also apart. Because of the uneven burl base, a
clear plastic centre finder was used to determine
the best spots to drill the leg holes.
When the leg locations were marked a jig was
made to hold the bowl on the drill press at the
needed 15-degree angle. Holes were drilled and
over-length legs were then epoxied into them.
After the epoxy dried, the bowl was placed face
down on a level surface and the plane of each leg
end was transferred with a shop-made height
gauge. The legs were cut and then the ends were

The Stuart Batty 5" Round Universal Grinding
Platform (UGP)
At a recent demonstration and class led by Tom
Wirsing, I witnessed the Stuart Batty 5" Round Universal Grinding Platform (UGP) in action. Tom
sharpened several of his Negative Rake Scrapers
(NRS) multiple times, and it quickly became apparent that this grinding platform provided ease and
precision far superior to the Oneway's Wolverine
platform I had previously used.
In later discussions with Tom about his choice of
sharpening platform, he noted that the 5" round
UGP offered an extra inch of clearance before the
platform interfered with the tool handle, as compared to the 6" platform. Additionally, he found
that the round platform facilitated easier sideways
sweeping in an arc compared to the rectangular
platform.
Inspired by Tom's insights, I purchased the 5"
round UGP with the UGP standard base. The UGP
has two base options: its own UGP base or an
adapter for the Wolverine system. Initially, I was
concerned that the Wolverine adapter might not
provide the same stability as the UGP base, so I
purchased the UGP base. After my purchase, a fellow guild member shared his positive experience
using the Wolverine adapter and confirmed its
effectiveness. When I acquire a second UGP for the
other side of my grinder, I plan to opt for the Wolverine base, as it will allow me to continue using
the Wolverine platform for rough shaping gouges
and the UGP to rough shape NRS.
The primary advantage of the UGP over the Wolverine platform lies in its consistent distance
maintenance between the platform and the grinding wheel, regardless of the platform's angle. The
UGP changes its angle by rotating on an arc, while
the Wolverine pivots on a hinge. This consistency
eliminates the cumbersome process that requires
multiple adjustments of the platform angle and the
space between the platform and the wheel, which I
found particularly challenging with the Wolverine.
Using a gauge to set the sharpening angle on the
Wolverine requires three hands: one for adjusting
the pivot, one for adjusting the distance from the
(Continued on page 33)

November 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 33
wheel, and a third to hold the angle gauge. For
those who, like me, struggle with coordination, the
UGP offers a much simpler solution.
The UGP is designed with an undercut at the rear
of the platform, enabling it to be positioned within
a millimetre from the wheel, even at extreme angles. This feature, combined with its ability to pivot
on an arc, eliminates the need to adjust the gap
between the wheel and the platform across a wide
range of grinding angles. For example, when sharpening Negative Rake Scrapers at a 22.5° angle, the
platform remains clear of the wheel, even when
nearly vertical. Additionally, the platform can be
returned to a 90° position without requiring any
readjustment of the spacing. As a result, the gap
between the wheel and the platform consistently
remains approximately 1mm throughout its entire
range.
Having good gauges to use with your sharpening
platform makes the alignment process much more
repeatable. While I initially owned Glenn Lucas's
Scraper and Skew Sharpening Gauge (called the
Moby Jig), I also purchased Stuart Batty's gauges
(the three-pack was cheaper than buying any two)
when I purchased the UGP. I use the Stuart Batty
gauges to set the UGP to 20° to rough shape my
Tom Wirsing inspired NSR and then to 22.5° to add
a cutting bevel. For Glenn Lucas's French Curve
NRS, I use his Moby Jig to set angles of 66° on the
bottom and 33° on the top, and for the skews, I use
an angle of 44°. The USP allows me to use these
gauges quickly, accurately and without fuss.
The Stuart Batty UGP base is wider than the Wolverine base, and if you are retrofitting an existing
installation, as I did, some additional changes will
likely be required. Even though the UGP's height is
adjustable, I optimized its alignment by raising my
grinder an additional ½". Depending on the length
of your grinder's wheel shafts, you may also need
to make provision for the UGP's base slightly encroaching under the grinder. This encroachment
may not occur on a Rikon grinder (now the de facto
standard grinder), but it was an issue with my King
Canada grinder. You can see a full video of my installation on my YouTube channel @DGWorkshop,
where I show the changes I made when installing
the UGP - remember to Like and Subscribe.
In conclusion, the Stuart Batty 5" Round Universal
Grinding Platform has significantly improved my
sharpening experience. Its innovative design and
ease of use make it a valuable addition to any
woodturner's toolkit. I highly recommend it to anyone looking to simplify the alignment process and
achieve more consistent results.
I look forward to hearing your thoughts and experiences!

Reason Why You Need a Draw Bar:
We at the GVWG always talk about safe practices
when you are at the lathe. On that note, if you are
using any device on the headstock spindle that
could come flying off and cause damage to the
piece you are making, or worse than that, injure
you, you need to use a draw bar to secure that device. This article describes how I make them for my
Nova DVRxp wood lathe. This safety device mounts
on the outboard end of the headstock and perhaps
save you a serious injury.
Fixtures with different thread sizes or a lathe with a
different configuration will require a different draw
bar with different dimensions but the steps I describe here should apply. Note that draw bars of
this design will only work on a lathe with a hollow
spindle.
Some turners also make a draw bar for the tailstock in case they want to pull on a thin blank with
a Jacob’s chuck, i.e. if making you are a trembleur,
or a very thin finial. These steps should work if you
want to do that.
The design I describe here shows how I made a ¼” -
20 tpi draw bar for my lathe.
Specifications:
The finished Draw bar will be 3 ¾” long by 1 5/8”
diameter with a ½” diameter by 5/8” long spigot.
A ¼” dia. hole drilled will be drilled through the
centre of the piece for a ¼” diameter threaded rod
to go through to attach to the fixture mounted on
the headstock spindle.
Materials:
•
Hardwood Blank Size: 2” x 2” x 4 ½” long
•
¼” Threaded rod 13 ¾” long
•
¼” fender washer
•
¼” lock washer
•
¼” wing nut
Tools:
•
¾” Skew; 3/8” Spindle Gouge
•
Thin parting tool
•
Jacob’s Chuck
•
¼” long brad point drill bit
•
Hammer
•
Drive centre with a cone attachment
•
Live centre with a cone attachment
•
Two scroll chucks, one with 50 mm jaws and
another with 25mm spigot jaws. One chuck and
two sets of jaws will also work.
Turning the Wooden Part:
1. Dimple the centres on both ends of the 2” x 2”
x 4 ½” blank. Do NOT round off the blank.
2. Mount the end of the blank that will NOT have
the spigot in a scroll chuck with 50mm jaws.
Line it up using a centre point in a live centre in
the tailstock.
3. Mount a Jacob’s chuck in the tailstock. Using a
long ¼” dia. brad point bit, drill a hole all the
way through the blank. Don’t worry if the bit
wanders a little bit off centre. That will be compensated for later. Verify that the ¼” treaded
rod fits through the hole. Modify the hole size,
if necessary,
4. Remove the blank from the chuck. Replace the
chuck with a drive centre with a cone attachment in the headstock spindle. I used a OneWay live centre with the small cone attached
and prevented it from spinning by putting a
small bolt through the little hole in the side of
(Continued on page 38)
Draw Bar - 1/4” x 20 TPI

November 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 38
the live centre and tightened the nut to stop
the bolt from falling out.
5. Place a live centre with a cone in the tailstock. I
used another OneWay live centre with small
cone but any live centre with a cone will work.
6. Remount the blank between these cone centres. Using the drilled hole and cones to centre
the blank will make sure that the hole through
the draw bar will be centered and not offset if
the drilled hole wandered a little off centre.
Round off the blank to about 1 ¾” outside diameter. The finished diameter will be established later.
7. Make a small tenon to fit 25mm chuck jaws on
the end that will NOT have the spigot. Here’s
where two chucks come in handy. One with
50mm jaws for rounding off the blank, and another with 25mm jaws to do the final shaping.
Failing that, change the chuck jaws from the
50mm ones to the 25mm ones.
8. Mount the end with the tenon on the chuck to
do the final shaping of the piece. Bring the live
centre with the cone in the tailstock up for support. True up the outside to the finished 1 5/8”
diameter. Turn the ½” dia. x 5/8” long spigot.
9. Remove the chuck with the piece still in it and
verify that the spigot will fit into the outboard
end of the lathe headstock spindle. Replace the
chuck with the piece still in it back on the lathe
spindle and adjust the fit as necessary.
10. After it fits OK, part off the piece while shaping
the end to the 3 ¾” finished length.
Since this is a utility type of piece, I feel that the
finish off the tool is satisfactory, and that sanding
and finishing is not necessary.
Assembly & Use:
Put the wing nut on one end of the piece of threaded rod. Hold the piece of threaded rod securely
and rivet over that end with a hammer. This is to
stop the wing nut from unthreading during use.
Place the lock washer, the flat washer, and then
the wooden piece with the spigot facing to the
right. The draw bar is now ready for use.
Slide threaded rod into the lathe outboard spindle.
The spigot end slides into the ½” hole in the headstock spindle and threads into the ¼” threaded end
on the fixture to be held in place.

 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock

with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.

electric cords for damage. Avoid the

 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
